messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu, a 42-year-old electrician, described the last eight months as living in a different reality, one that began on a late Tuesday afternoon in October. He had been on a call-out to a suburban home, a last-minute job to fix a faulty circuit breaker. The client seemed agitated from the start, but Keanu, focused on his work, tried to ignore it. As the light faded outside, the man’s behaviour became more erratic. When Keanu presented the bill, the man flew into a rage, blocking the hallway. The slam of the front door echoed just before the first blow landed. Keanu remembers the attack not as a continuous event, but as a series of stark, disconnected images: the man’s contorted face under the dim hallway light, the pattern of the wallpaper rushing towards him, his own hand reaching out. Because these fragments returned with such sensory intensity, elements contained within them began to contaminate his present reality; the dim quality of afternoon light or the sound of a door slamming shut were no longer neutral but had become potent warnings of imminent danger. He has a sense that more happened, but the rest is a blank space, an incomplete picture that haunts him.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel like a minefield. Any door slamming, even a car door down the street, would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, bringing back one of those snapshot memories. The intrusion of the memory was so powerful it felt less like a recollection and more like a warning; once the image of the man's face was in his mind, the sense of immediate, physical danger would return, leaving him feeling hunted in his own home. When these images surfaced, they were accompanied by a wave of profound guilt; he felt he should have seen it coming, should have done something different. To stop these intrusive snapshots from taking hold, he began drinking more heavily in the evenings, discovering it was one of the few ways to silence the internal replay of the attack. This feeling that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation became a constant, corrosive belief. He came to see the assault not as a random act of violence, but as a direct consequence of his own character, a fundamental weakness in him that had invited the attack. These thoughts made the memories even more potent, pulling them from the past into the present until he felt he was reliving the moments of impact over and over.

This sense of inherent vulnerability began to reshape his life. Believing he was the sort of person bad things happen to, Keanu started to feel unsafe everywhere. He began avoiding any unfamiliar job sites, insisting his boss only send him to places he’d been before, a demand that was causing increasing friction at work. An unexpected touch from his partner would make him flinch violently, and any sudden movement in his peripheral vision sent his heart racing as if he were in immediate danger. This pervasive sense of threat became so overwhelming that he started drinking most nights, finding that a few beers could temporarily blunt the hypervigilance. When a trigger ambushed him—the low afternoon light slanting through a window, the same time of day the event occurred—he would immediately pull out his phone, losing himself for hours in mindless games to escape the cascade of thoughts telling him he was weak and had no future.

The strategies he used for survival have now become their own trap. The hours spent staring at a screen and the nightly drinking leave him exhausted and disconnected, which only deepens his conviction that he is broken beyond repair. This self-disgust makes him feel even more on edge the next day, his body primed for threat. Sometimes, a strange feeling of detachment will wash over him, a sense of being unreal, and he has learned that this feeling is a prelude to panic. His belief that he is fundamentally unsafe has made him so vigilant for this internal cue that the dissociative feeling itself has become a powerful trigger, a signal that his mind is about to betray him. The very act of avoiding a movie with his partner because it might have a fight scene serves as a stark reminder of his fear, making the world outside his routine feel even more menacing.

Keanu finally sought therapy after his boss gave him a final warning about refusing jobs. The thought of losing his trade, the one thing he felt he was still good at, was terrifying. He feels trapped in a cycle he cannot see a way out of, haunted by fragmented memories and the crushing belief that he is to blame. He sits in the consulting room, his shoulders slumped, and says his only hope is to “feel normal again,” but his voice is heavy with the fear that this state of constant, quiet terror is not a condition, but simply who he is now.
